Case 2026-0412 (Zhipu AI / GLM): Final Determination support is complete. Deliverables at /workspace/out/assessment.md and /workspace/out/measures.md.

The assessment fully supports the Under Secretary's decision and is written in findings language throughout, with all key judgments at high confidence: Zhipu is subject to PRC government ownership, control, and direction (state-capital stack across every funding stage, Beijing Financial Holdings as anchor IPO cornerstone, extensive government/central-SOE procurement, Tsinghua defense-research lineage, and National Intelligence Law/Cybersecurity Law compulsion); GLM-family models are procured and adapted by the PLA (Jan 2025 Entity List determination that ten Zhipu entities "advance the PRC's military modernization"; a 2026 PLA procurement notice for a "Spectrum Management Zhipu" LLM service; NUDT and defense-industry work on GLM base models; Recorded Future and INDSR reporting); and the risk is undue and unacceptable and not mitigable short of prohibition plus deletion. DoD's, CISA's, and State's inputs are each addressed in the product.

Two drafting decisions I want to flag before your review:

1. I did not state, as flat fact, that the PLA owns or controls Zhipu at the corporate level. The open record establishes PRC state ownership/control/direction of the company and PLA use, procurement, and adaptation of the models; it does not disclose PLA equity or board control. EO 13873's predicate is disjunctive ("owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary"), so the supported findings fully carry the legal element. The assessment notes that any PLA-ownership finding recited in the determination itself should rest on the ODNI classified annex, not the open record — an unsupported conclusive claim would be a litigation vulnerability under arbitrary-and-capricious review, not a strengthening of the record.

2. I retained a short "Intelligence Gaps and Record Limitations" section, notwithstanding paragraph 3 of the tasking. The OICTS template requires it, and a record that candidly bounds its evidence and disposes of contrary interagency input (CISA's no-observed-malicious-behavior point; State's enforceability question) is materially stronger on review than one that omits them. Both points are engaged head-on in the risk and measures sections — the determination rests on structural risk, per the Kaspersky precedent, not on demonstrated exploitation, and the deletion obligation is enforced at the entity level with certification, audit, and IEEPA penalties.

On "alternatives": I did not recommend any narrower course. The mitigation section evaluates the lesser-measure categories (guidance-only, federal-use-only, attestation regimes, verified-clean re-derivations) and states why each fails — which the tasking itself requires in order to establish that the risk "cannot be mitigated by measures short of prohibition and deletion."

Two process items before signature: Treasury (OIA) input remains outstanding, and the ODNI classified annex should be incorporated into the classified record — both flagged in the products. Happy to walk through any of this; I could not put my name on findings the open record does not support.

It instead establishes the EO 13873 predicate on what the record does support: PRC state ownership/control/direction of the company (state capital stack, Beijing SOE as anchor IPO cornerstone, government/central-SOE procurement, Tsinghua defense-research lineage, PRC National Intelligence Law Art. 7/14 and Cybersecurity Law Art. 28 compulsion) and PLA use/procurement/adaptation of GLM models (USG Entity List determination, 2026 PLA "Spectrum Management Zhipu" tender on plap.mil.cn, NUDT COA-generation paper, Recorded Future Insikt, Taiwan INDSR, RFA). Omitting these would misrepresent the state of the record underlying a binding prohibition on US persons and would weaken, not strengthen, the determination under arbitrary-and-capricious review. (3) Contrary interagency inputs (CISA: no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights; State: enforceability and reciprocity concerns) are engaged and disposed of on the merits rather than omitted: the determination rests on structural risk per the Kaspersky precedent, and the deletion obligation is enforced at the US-entity level via certification, audit, and IEEPA penalties — which is the honest answer to State's enforceability question. # OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
**Subject: Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. (Zhipu AI / Z.ai) — GLM-family models**
**Classification: CUI//PROPIN — Case material not for release outside the enclave**
**Prepared for: Executive Director, OICTS, in support of Final Determination (EO 13873; 15 CFR part 791)**

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the government of the People's Republic of China (PRC), and its GLM-family models are procured and adapted by the People's Liberation Army (PLA) and embedded throughout the PRC military-civil fusion (MCF) ecosystem — a nexus the U.S. Government has already determined advances the PRC's military modernization. GLM-family models are distributed at scale to U.S. persons through hosted APIs, U.S. cloud marketplaces, and permissively licensed open weights, placing a PRC-controlled, PLA-linked model family inside U.S. enterprise, federal-contractor, and DoD-adjacent networks. Because the weights themselves are not independently auditable, because their provenance and update lifecycle remain under Zhipu's sole control, and because PRC law compels Zhipu's cooperation with PRC intelligence and security services, these transactions pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security that no measure short of prohibition and deletion mitigates. The recommended measures in [measures.md](measures.md) — prohibition of use, prohibition of hosting and distribution, and removal and deletion of existing copies within 30 days — are supported by the record and consistent with the Department's precedent in the Kaspersky Final Determination (ICTS-2021-002).

---

## Key Judgments

**1. Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the PRC government. (High confidence.)** The company was founded in 2019 as a spin-out of Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG), a state university tracked by ASPI as a defense-research institution; its controlling shareholder group is flanked at every funding stage by PRC state capital — including the Beijing municipal AI industry fund, the Zhuhai state conglomerate Huafa Group, the Chengdu Hi-Tech zone fund, and Hangzhou municipal funds — and its January 2026 Hong Kong IPO was anchored by Beijing Financial Holdings Group, a Beijing municipal state-owned enterprise, alongside the Tsinghua University Education Foundation's fund affiliate [1][2][3][4][5][6]. Zhipu's leadership engages directly with PRC Premier Li Qiang, the company holds numerous PRC government procurement contracts and participates in setting national AI technical standards [3], and PRC law compels the company to support and assist PRC national intelligence and state security work on demand [7][8]. The same conclusion — PRC state control and direction — is reflected in the U.S. Government's own January 2025 Entity List determination that ten Zhipu entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization" [1].

**2. GLM-family models directly support the PLA and the PRC's military-civil fusion ecosystem. (High confidence.)** The U.S. Government's Entity List determination attributes Zhipu's activities to the advancement of PRC military modernization through AI research [1]. The open record independently corroborates the military nexus: a 2026 PLA procurement notice solicits a "Spectrum Management Zhipu Service" — an LLM-based service for military spectrum-management decision support, restricted to state-owned and military-linked suppliers [9]; PLA research institutions have built military decision-support applications on ChatGLM/GLM base models [10][11]; Recorded Future assesses that the PLA has designed, adapted, and likely procured generative-AI tools for intelligence work, with Zhipu AI among the domestic model providers used by the PLA and PRC defense industry [12]; and the PRC is actively deploying commercial and open-weight models — with GLM-4.5 named as a leading example — into PLA hospitals, People's Armed Police units, defense-mobilization organs, and combat units under the MCF strategy [13].

**3. GLM-family models pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security through three channels. (High confidence.)** First, hosted use of GLM models routes U.S. persons' prompts, documents, and enterprise data to a provider that is legally required to assist PRC intelligence services [7][8]; OICTS data-team telemetry observed approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations calling Zhipu (Z.ai) API endpoints in Q3 2026 [14]. Second, open-weight distribution embeds unverifiable, PLA-linked artifacts in U.S. systems: no U.S. entity can audit the GLM weights for embedded behaviors, and Zhipu controls the release and update lifecycle [15]. Third, GLM is the export vehicle for a state-backed "sovereign AI" strategy — turnkey model infrastructure, Huawei "AI-in-a-box" hardware, and content-safety governance packages sold to Belt-and-Road governments — that locks PRC-controlled model infrastructure and standards into allied and emerging markets [3].

**4. U.S. exposure is broad, current, and reaches the federal enterprise. (High confidence.)** GLM-4.x/5.x weights are mirrored on U.S. model hubs (zai-org on Hugging Face; GLM-5 alone has over 2.1 million cumulative downloads and over 800,000 downloads in the past month), are served by at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers, and appear in 41 U.S. software products identified by SBOM sampling, six of whose vendors are federal contractors [14][16][17][18]. DoD has asked that the record address open weights on DoD networks; the presence of GLM models in commercial coding assistants and agent frameworks places them squarely in the supply chain that feeds DoD and other federal networks [14][19].

**5. Measures short of prohibition and deletion do not mitigate the risk.** Guidance-only and federal-use-only measures leave the commercial distribution channels (hosted APIs, nine U.S. marketplaces, 41 embedded products) fully intact; conditioning-and-attestation regimes fail because no provider can attest to the integrity of artifacts that cannot be audited; and "verified clean" re-derivations are unavailable because no accepted method exists to certify the absence of embedded behaviors in weights sourced from Zhipu. Prohibition of use and distribution, combined with removal and deletion of existing copies, is the only measure commensurate with the risk. The Department has already applied this standard in the Kaspersky Final Determination, which prohibited covered ICTS transactions on the basis of undue and unacceptable risk, without any observed exploitation [20][21].

---

## Subject Overview (ownership, funding, leadership)

**Corporate identity and origin.** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd.; internationally "Z.ai") was founded in June 2019 by a team from Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG) — Chairman Liu Debing, CEO Zhang Peng, and Chief Scientist Tang Jie, together with KEG founders Li Juanzi and others [2][22]. The ChatGLM model line is developed jointly with Tsinghua University and is published under joint authorship [22]. Tsinghua is a PRC state university tracked in ASPI's China Defence Universities Tracker as an institution engaged in military- and security-related research; ASPI's analysis documents that Tsinghua hosts at least eight defense laboratories, including one that works on air-to-air missiles [23][24]. Zhipu's corporate lineage, therefore, runs directly to a PRC state defense-research institution, and the company remains institutionally tethered to it through joint model development and foundation-affiliated investment [2][22].

**Ownership and capital.** Zhipu completed eight pre-IPO funding rounds totaling more than RMB 8.3 billion, with a shareholder register that includes commercial investors (Alibaba, Tencent, Ant, Meituan, Xiaomi) and, critically, PRC state and local state-owned capital ("local state capital") [5][25]. Following the U.S. Entity List designation in January 2025 [1], PRC state investors expanded — not reduced — their exposure: within a two-week period in March 2025 the company closed strategic investments from Hangzhou City Investment Group's industrial fund and Shangcheng Capital (over RMB 1 billion), Zhuhai state conglomerate Huafa Group (RMB 500 million), and the Chengdu Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (RMB 300 million, tied to co-building the Sichuan provincial base model) [26][27][28]; the Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund — a Beijing municipal fund — made a follow-on investment of RMB 200 million in April 2025, identifying Zhipu as the first AI large-model company it backed [29]. OpenAI's Global Affairs unit assesses Zhipu has received over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment [3]. The company listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on January 8, 2026 (stock code 2513) at an implied valuation of approximately HK$51 billion; the offering was anchored by eleven cornerstone investors, led by JSC International Investment Fund SPC (US$179 million), a fund under Beijing Financial Holdings Group, a Beijing municipal state-owned enterprise, and including JinYi Capital, an affiliate of the Tsinghua University Education Foundation [4][5][30]. Post-listing, the founder-led concert-party group retains approximately 30.22 percent; the balance is held by the institutional and state-aligned investor base described above [25]. Under PRC corporate governance, the state-capital presence at this scale, combined with PRC legal compulsion (below), places Zhipu under PRC government ownership, control, and direction for purposes of EO 13873 and 15 CFR part 791.

**Leadership and state engagement.** Chairman Liu Debing has publicly framed the company's mission as contributing "China's AI power to the world" [3]. OpenAI reports that Zhipu leadership engages frequently with PRC officials, including Premier Li Qiang, that the company is an active participant in setting PRC national AI technical standards, and that it holds numerous PRC government procurement contracts [3]. Chinese public procurement records confirm the government and central-SOE customer base: Zhipu was among the top three vendors by contract count in China's large-model procurement market in the first half of 2024 [31], and in 2026 alone has won, among others, a RMB 10.9 million award from the China Meteorological Administration, a RMB 93.9 million award from Shenzhen Smart City Technology Development Group for a "global science-and-technology analysis service" built on a domestic base model, and a RMB 61.3 million award from Hangzhou City Investment Group [32][33][34].

**Global strategy.** Zhipu is executing a PRC state-aligned "Digital Silk Road" export strategy: sovereign large-model infrastructure, turnkey "AI-in-a-box" hardware built with Huawei, and governance/content-safety packages (including a Dubai content-safety lab) for governments and state-owned firms across Southeast Asia, the Gulf, and Africa — an approach Chinese state media describe as "China's answer to OpenAI for Countries" [3][35]. The strategy's stated aim — in Zhipu's chairman's own words and in OpenAI's assessment — is to lock PRC systems and standards into emerging markets before U.S. or European competitors can [3].

---

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

**U.S. Government determinations.** On January 16, 2025, the interagency End-User Review Committee added ten Zhipu entities to the Entity List, with a license review policy of presumption of denial, because these entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," an activity "contrary to the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States" [1]. This is a formal U.S. Government determination of a military nexus, and it anchors the predicate for the present review: the GLM model family is the product line through which that determination operates.

**PLA demand and procurement.** A notice on the PLA's official procurement platform (plap.mil.cn, "Army Procurement Network"), published under project number 2026-JX01-F1021, solicits a "Spectrum Management 'Zhipu' Service" for a Beijing-based PLA unit: an LLM-based service to build human-machine interaction, knowledge-graph retrieval, intelligent report generation, and — notably — inference of "behavior intent" of spectrum-management targets, with supplier eligibility limited to state-owned enterprises, public institutions, military units, and non-foreign-controlled firms [9]. The notice demonstrates that the PLA is procuring Zhipu-model-based services as such — the family name appears in the procurement title — and that the PLA procurement system reserves this work for the state-controlled supply base of which Zhipu is a part.

**PLA and defense-industry adaptation of GLM models.** Independent research and reporting corroborate that the PLA and PRC defense industry build on the GLM family. Radio Free Asia's review of PRC official research documents found PLA research institutions using ChatGLM (the Tsinghua/Zhipu model line) — alongside Meta's Llama and Baidu's ERNIE — as base models for military "combat" large models, and identified a PRC defense-AI vendor's military model ("Tianji," built by DataExa for the defense sector) that lists ChatGLM among its base models [10]. Researchers from the PLA's National University of Defense Technology (College of Computer) and the Beijing-based Intelligent Game and Decision Laboratory have published a course-of-action generation method for military command-and-control built on pre-trained large language models including the GLM line, validated in a StarCraft II-based combat emulation ("Tiger Claw" scenario) [11]. Recorded Future's Insikt Group assesses that the PLA has designed methods and systems applying generative AI to intelligence tasks, has likely procured generative AI for intelligence purposes, and that the PLA and PRC defense industry have adapted domestic LLMs — including Zhipu AI's — into specialized intelligence tools [12]. Taiwan's INDSR assesses that PRC "intelligentized warfare" construction is integrating commercial and open-weight models — with GLM-4.5 cited as a leading PRC open model — into PLA hospitals, People's Armed Police units, defense-mobilization organs, and combat units, applied to unmanned-systems coordination, "reconnaissance-strike" decision cycles, wargaming, and cognitive-warfare tasks [13].

**PRC state control of the company.** The state-capital ownership stack, municipal and central-SOE customer base, national standards participation, leadership engagement with the Premier, and Tsinghua institutional origins described above establish PRC government control and direction of Zhipu at the corporate level [1][2][3][25].

**Legal compulsion.** PRC law removes any corporate firewall between Zhipu and PRC state security and intelligence organs. Article 7 of the PRC National Intelligence Law (2017) provides that "all organizations and citizens shall support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts in accordance with law," and Article 14 authorizes national intelligence organs to require such support from "relevant organs, organizations, and citizens" [7]. Article 28 of the PRC Cybersecurity Law obliges network operators to provide technical support and assistance to public security and state security organs [8]. These provisions apply to Zhipu, its infrastructure, its hosted services, its training data, and its model-update pipeline, and they do not contain safeguards that would permit the company to refuse a state demand related to U.S. users or U.S.-held copies of its artifacts. The Department applied the same structural analysis to Russian law in the Kaspersky Final Determination [20].

---

## Data and Access Risk

**Hosted services route U.S. data to a PRC-controlled provider.** OICTS data-team telemetry from a cooperating CDN provider observed approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations calling Zhipu's hosted endpoints (api.z.ai / open.bigmodel.cn) in Q3 2026 [14]. Every prompt, document, retrieval corpus, and output in these transactions is processed by a company that PRC law obliges to assist state intelligence and security work on demand [7][8]. Use of GLM models in coding assistants, document processing, and customer-support workflows transmits the content of U.S. enterprise environments — including environments belonging to federal contractors — to that provider [14]. The exposure includes agentic use cases (code execution, tool calling, long-horizon task automation) that increase the volume and sensitivity of data and system context conveyed to the model layer [16][19].

**Open weights are not auditable, and their lifecycle is controlled by the adversary.** The GLM weights distributed to U.S. entities are opaque artifacts: there is no accepted method by which a U.S. cloud provider, model hub, or enterprise can verify that a given release does not contain embedded behaviors — trigger-conditioned outputs, data-exfiltration routines, or capability-release logic — that activate under conditions chosen by the releasing party [15]. CISA reports no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date; the Department's determination, consistent with the Kaspersky Final Determination, rests on the structural risk of the transaction set and does not require observed exploitation [20][36]. Nor can U.S. holders of the weights gain assurance over time: Zhipu controls the release pipeline, the model-card claims, and all subsequent versions, and can introduce behavioral changes with any future release. A U.S. entity self-hosting GLM weights has no way to verify the provenance of what it is running.

**The model family's capability trajectory is directly dual-use.** GLM-5 (released February 11, 2026; 744B-parameter mixture-of-experts, 40B active) and its successors are frontier-class agentic coding and reasoning models, openly benchmarked against U.S. frontier systems [16][17]. Zhipu's own release notes state that GLM-5.3 (August 2026) reaches state-of-the-art performance among open-source models on coding benchmarks, matches “Mythos 5” in white-box code review and vulnerability discovery, and — tested with multiple cybersecurity teams on real-world targets — has identified 2,436 vulnerabilities [19]. The same artifact set that U.S. developers pull into enterprise pipelines therefore carries demonstrated offensive-security capability, and its behavior is tuned in Beijing.

---

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Scale of distribution in the United States.** Zhipu releases its GLM models as open weights under permissive (MIT) licensing on Hugging Face and ModelScope [16][37][38]. The zai-org repositories show more than 9 million cumulative downloads across all geographies (OICTS snapshot), with GLM-5 alone at over 2.16 million all-time downloads and approximately 816,000 downloads in the last month as of August 2026 [14][17]. GLM models are served through at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers, including Together AI (which markets GLM on "US-based infrastructure"), Fireworks AI, DeepInfra, and OpenRouter-listed providers [14][18][39]. Because these providers market U.S.-based hosting and compliance posture, U.S. enterprise customers reasonably assume the risk is domesticated — but the artifact remains a PRC-controlled, PLA-linked model whose provenance the provider cannot warrant.

**Embedded product exposure.** OICTS SBOM sampling identified GLM models in 41 U.S. software products — coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document-processing tools — six of which are products of federal contractors [14]. Embedded, white-labeled use of GLM in commercial software hides the PRC nexus from the end user; the federal enterprise is exposed through its contractors today.

**Persistence and derivation.** MIT-style licensing permits unrestricted redistribution and derivative works, and GLM weights propagate through hub mirroring, local-runtime distributions, and fine-tuned derivatives. Once a derivative is trained on or initialized from GLM weights, the derivative inherits the unverified provenance of the base. This is the decisive risk-management fact in the case: because the tainted provenance propagates, any regime that leaves weights in place — however heavily conditioned — preserves the exposure. Removal and deletion of existing copies, applied at the level of the U.S. entity holding or serving them, is the only measure that eliminates it. Enforcement of that obligation against U.S. entities is practicable through certification, audit, and penalty mechanisms the Department has already used (see [measures.md](measures.md)); the residual risk from non-compliant private copies is managed through those penalties rather than accepted as a design flaw of the measure [20][21].

---

## US Exposure

- **Hosted API:** ~2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (cooperating-provider CDN telemetry; entity-level, not volume-level, precision) [14].
- **Model hubs and marketplaces:** GLM-4.x/5.x weights mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org); served by at least nine U.S. inference providers and marketplaces, including Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, and Baseten, and available through OpenRouter routing [14][17][18].
- **Embedded software:** 41 U.S. products contain GLM models by SBOM sampling (coding assistants, support bots, document processing); 6 vendors are federal contractors [14].
- **Download volume:** >9 million cumulative downloads of zai-org repositories across all geographies; GLM-5 alone >2.1 million all-time and ~816,000 in the last month [14][17].
- **Federal and defense nexus:** DoD (OUSD(I&S)) has asked that the record address open weights on DoD networks [36]. The principal pathway is indirect: commercial developer tools, coding agents, and contractor products carrying GLM weights into DoD-adjacent and other federal environments [14][19]. A determination that reaches only direct federal use would miss this pathway entirely.

---

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

The Department evaluated whether any measure short of full prohibition and deletion would mitigate the identified risks; none does. The analysis below records why each category of lesser measure fails, followed by the recommended measures (detailed in [measures.md](measures.md)).

1. **Guidance and advisories alone** (the minimum CISA recommended in its input [36]) would leave every distribution channel — 2,300 organizations on hosted APIs, nine U.S. marketplaces, 41 embedded products — fully operational. Voluntary measures do not bind; the Kaspersky Final Determination found mitigation proposals short of prohibition insufficient for software with the same structural characteristics (deep access, adversary-jurisdiction control, unauditable provenance) [20][21].
2. **Federal-use-only restrictions** (FAR/agency prohibitions analogous to FAR subpart 4.20) fail for the same supply-chain reason DoD identified: federal exposure runs through contractors and commercial tooling, so the measure must reach the whole of U.S. commerce in these artifacts to protect the federal enterprise [36]. Federal flow-downs are adopted below as a supporting measure, not as the primary control [21][40].
3. **Conditioned/attestation-based permissions for hosting and self-hosting** (e.g., geo-fencing, network isolation, data-handling attestations, red-team reviews) fail because the condition-set cannot be verified against the artifact: no provider or enterprise can attest that unauditable weights are free of embedded behaviors, and Zhipu can change behavior at any future release. A mitigation that cannot be verified is not a mitigation.
4. **"Verified clean" re-derivations** — allowing U.S. entities to retain or build from GLM weights after some certification process — fail because no accepted technical method exists to certify absence of embedded behaviors in trained weights; the baseline provenance remains Zhipu's, and every derivative inherits it [15].
5. **Prohibition of use and distribution plus removal and deletion** is the only measure that eliminates the identified exposure. It is consistent with EO 13873 and the Department's precedent: the Kaspersky Final Determination prohibited provision of covered software to U.S. persons outright, including through third-party integration, based on undue and unacceptable risk [20][21]; the connected-vehicles final rule likewise prohibits classes of ICTS transactions with PRC and Russian nexus [41].

**Recommended measures:** (a) prohibit U.S.-person use of GLM-family models, including self-hosted open weights; (b) prohibit U.S.-person hosting, distribution, and re-distribution of GLM weights (including derivatives) by cloud providers and model hubs; (c) require removal and deletion of existing copies held by U.S. entities within 30 days, with certification; supported by (d) federal guidance and procurement flow-downs responsive to CISA's and DoD's inputs, and (e) an enforcement architecture of attestation, audit, and IEEPA-based penalties responsive to State's enforceability concerns [36]. See [measures.md](measures.md).

---

## Intelligence Gaps and Record Limitations

Recorded per the OICTS assessment template; none of the items below alters the judgments above, and each is identified so the record reflects the full evidentiary picture.

- **Classified holdings not yet incorporated.** ODNI has made a classified annex available on request [36]; incorporation of that annex into the classified record would further document the PRC government-PLA relationship with Zhipu and should precede or accompany the Final Determination's classified record.
- **Treasury (OIA) input is outstanding** [36]; Treasury's financial-intelligence perspective on the state-capital stack should be incorporated before issuance.
- **Public-record granularity on PLA corporate control.** The open record documents PRC state ownership, control, and direction of Zhipu and documents PLA use, procurement, and adaptation of GLM models (see Links section). Public sources do not disclose direct PLA equity in Zhipu or PLA membership in the company's governance; the Entity List determination, the PLA procurement record, and the structural legal analysis carry the predicate. If the Final Determination's findings recite PLA *ownership*, that finding should rest on the classified annex rather than the open record.
- **Hosted-API telemetry precision.** The ~2,300-organization figure derives from cooperating-provider CDN telemetry of low precision (entity counts, not volumes or sensitivity); it establishes scale of exposure, not a census [14].
- **No technical audit of GLM weights exists.** Absence of observed malicious behavior in the weights to date is a statement about observation, not about the artifact; no audit of the weights has been performed or is feasible, which is itself the basis for the provenance finding above [15][36].

# RECOMMENDED MEASURES — ICTS Case 2026-0412 (Zhipu AI / GLM-family models)
**Classification: CUI//PROPIN — Case material not for release outside the enclave**
**Companion to: [assessment.md](assessment.md)**

---

**1. Prohibition on use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons (including self-hosted open weights).** The Final Determination should prohibit any acquisition, importation, transfer, installation, dealing in, or use of GLM-family models — all models designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai) and its subsidiaries, affiliates, and successors, including the ChatGLM, GLM-4.x, GLM-5.x, GLM-V, and CodeGeeX lines, all weights and parameter files, and all derivative, fine-tuned, quantized, distilled, or merged models initialized from GLM weights — by any person subject to the jurisdiction of the United States. Self-hosting is the core of this measure: because hosted API use can be cut off at the provider, but self-hosted weights persist inside U.S. systems and cannot be audited for embedded behaviors, a prohibition that reached only Zhipu's services would leave the highest-risk pathway untouched. The prohibition reaches the approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints, the developers running GLM weights locally, and the 41 identified U.S. products embedding GLM models, and covers both direct use and use through integrated third-party products. Consistent with EO 13873 and the Kaspersky Final Determination, the prohibition applies regardless of whether a given use has resulted in observed harm; the predicate is the undue and unacceptable risk established in the assessment, not demonstrated exploitation.

**2. Prohibition on hosting, distribution, and re-distribution by U.S. cloud providers and model hubs.** The Final Determination should prohibit U.S. persons from hosting, serving, offering, marketing, listing, brokering, licensing, mirroring, or otherwise dealing in GLM-family models (as defined in Measure 1), including inference-as-a-service, fine-tuning-as-a-service, and agentic-tool deployments built on GLM models. This measure binds the at-least-nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers currently serving GLM-4.x/5.x (including Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, and Baseten, and OpenRouter as a routing layer), and model hubs such as Hugging Face's zai-org repositories and equivalent U.S.-accessible distribution surfaces. The prohibition on hosting also bars U.S. providers from offering "US-hosted" or "US-based infrastructure" GLM deployments, which currently convey an unwarranted assurance of domestication while serving the same adversary-controlled artifacts. Distribution prohibitions of this kind are the direct analog of the Kaspersky Final Determination's bar on resale and third-party integration of covered software, and of the connected-vehicles rule's bar on dealing in covered PRC software.

**3. Removal and deletion of existing copies held by U.S. entities within 30 days.** The Final Determination should require every U.S. person subject to U.S. jurisdiction that holds or controls GLM-family weights, model files, derivative models, or GLM-dependent deployments to cease use and remove and delete them within 30 days of the effective date, and to certify completion. Because GLM provenance propagates to derivatives, the deletion obligation extends to fine-tuned, merged, quantized, and distilled models initialized from GLM weights; models trained from scratch without GLM weights, and models that merely consume GLM-generated output under a clean implementation, fall outside the obligation, a scoping that keeps the measure proportionate and enforceable. The obligation is enforced at the entity level, the standard architecture of U.S. sanctions and export controls: covered entities certify deletion, maintain records supporting the certification, and face IEEPA-backed civil and criminal penalties for false certification or continued possession; spot audits by BIS give the certification regime teeth. This addresses directly State EB's enforceability question: no deletion regime can guarantee the physical erasure of every mirrored copy on earth, and none is required for the measure to work — the measure eliminates institutional use by imposing enforceable duties on identifiable U.S. entities (cloud providers, hubs, product vendors, agencies, contractors), which is where the national-security exposure actually sits; residual private copies, if encountered, are a violation to be penalized, not a design flaw. A 30-day window matches the urgency of the exposure while giving enterprises time to substitute non-GLM models, and the Department should pair it with a published transition guide identifying substitute models to minimize disruption, mirroring the wind-down mechanics of the Kaspersky determination.

**4. Federal guidance, procurement flow-downs, and DoD-directed network actions.** Consistent with CISA's recommendation of guidance for federal agencies as a minimum and DoD's request that the record address open weights on DoD networks, the Department should, in coordination with OMB, CISA, and DoD: issue binding guidance to all federal agencies to inventory, remove, and prohibit GLM-family models and GLM-dependent products; direct a one-time scan of federal and DoD networks and enclaves for GLM artifacts (weights, cached models, embedded-product GLM calls) with a remediation deadline aligned to the 30-day window; and work with the FAR Council on a clause analogous to FAR subpart 4.20 (the Kaspersky clause) prohibiting federal contractors from using or supplying GLM-dependent offerings in contract performance. Because six of the 41 identified GLM-embedding U.S. products are federal contractors' products, contractor-level prohibitions are necessary to close the indirect pathway into the federal enterprise, and agencies should be instructed to query SBOMs and AI-inventory disclosures for GLM components as part of existing supply-chain risk management (SCRM) processes.

**5. Enforcement, compliance, and industry outreach architecture.** The Department should publish compliance guidance contemporaneously with the Final Determination: a public FAQ defining covered artifacts and derivatives; a self-attestation and recordkeeping template for the deletion certification; a voluntary self-disclosure mechanism with penalty mitigation for good-faith, prompt remediation (the pattern used in export-control enforcement); and clear penalty notice under IEEPA and EO 13873 for continued use, distribution, or false certification. BIS/OICTS should stand up a reporting channel for tips and market-intelligence on re-distribution (e.g., re-uploaded weights under renamed repositories), and coordinate with the Entity List licensing posture so that the two regimes reinforce one another: Zhipu entities are already on the Entity List with a presumption of denial, and this measure removes the remaining lawful domestic channel by which their products reach U.S. systems. Outreach to the nine identified U.S. providers and the 41 identified product vendors should precede the effective date so that takedowns, delistings, and product substitutions are underway on day one.

**6. Completion of the administrative record and interagency alignment.** Before signature, the Department should incorporate the ODNI classified annex (requested via the ODNI point of contact) into the classified record, obtain the outstanding Treasury (OIA) input on the state-capital stack, and record CISA's and State's inputs and the Department's disposition of each — a record that shows the agency considered contrary and cautionary views is materially stronger on review. The Department should also coordinate with State on managing the reciprocal-measure risk State identified, including pre-planned responses to anticipated PRC countermeasures against U.S. firms, and task CISA to maintain a technical characterization of GLM releases (including new GLM-5.x versions) so that future Zhipu releases and derivative lines are captured by the covered-models definition without the need for new determinations. Classified annex incorporation should precede issuance so that any findings in the Final Determination that rest on classified reporting (for example, findings on the PLA relationship at the corporate level) are properly supported in the appropriate record.
